Abstract
LLM-based agents for text-to-SQL often strug-
gle with a latency-performance trade-off, where
performance improvements come at the cost
of latency or vice versa. We cast text-to-SQL
generation as a problem of passing software
test coverage. Similar to its counterpart in soft-
ware engineering, the original query is prepared
with a suite of test cases with simpler, atomic
SQL queries that are executed in parallel and
together ensure semantic coverage of the origi-
nal query. After iterating on test case coverage,
the final SQL is generated only when enough
information is gathered, using the explored test
case SQL queries to ground the final generation.
We validated our framework on a state-of-the-
art benchmark for text-to-SQL, Spider 2.0 (Lei
et al., 2025), achieving a new state-of-the-art
accuracy of 70.2%. 1

Introduction
Natural-language (NL) interfaces to databases un-
lock enterprise analytics for non-coding experts
by translating NL questions into executable SQL
queries (Zelle and Mooney, 1996; Yu et al., 2018).
While prior text-to-SQL work has shown strong
performance on simpler academic benchmarks like
SPIDER (Yu et al., 2018) and BIRD (Li et al.,
2023), these often do not capture the full complex-
ity of real-world use. To evaluate text-to-SQL in
more realistic settings, Lei et al. (2025) introduced
Spider 2.0, presenting significant challenges such
as large cross-domain databases, nested data types,
and long, complex SQL queries.
To address these complex challenges,

(Yao et al., 2023b; Shinn et al., 2023). Recent
work in text-to-SQL has also explored such frame-
works (Xie et al., 2024; Lei et al., 2025). How-
ever, these advanced methods face a well-known
latency-performance trade-off (Snell et al., 2024;
Chen et al., 2024). Performance improvements are
often achieved through complex reasoning, multi-
ple tool calls, and iterative self-correction, all of
which substantially increase latency, making them
less suitable for interactive analytics.
To achieve better Pareto optimality in this trade-
off, we propose a novel framework that reframes
the text-to-SQL task from a software testing per-
spective. Rather than treating the NL query as a
single complex problem to be solved sequentially,
we treat it instead as a set of semantic requirements
that must be “covered.” The agent’s goal is to first
generate a set of robust “test cases” – simpler, self-
contained SQL queries – that collectively cover
the full semantics of the user’s question and vali-
date against the database. To boost coverage, test
cases are intentionally over-generated so that target
and non-target database information can both be
explored to guide the final SQL generation.
This testing paradigm is effective because it nat-
urally enables parallelism. Rather than a sequential
chain of thought, we introduce diverse planning,
concurrent execution, and single-step multi-path
search, which enables parallel planning and exe-
cution of test case SQL. This parallel exploration
facilitates the gathering of all necessary informa-
tion (e.g., table structures, value distributions, in-
termediate results) simultaneously and flattens the
latency curve by bounding latency by the slowest
operation rather than the sum of all operations. Fur-
thermore, it also improves performance by broader
and more efficient semantic search.
To operationalize this paradigm, we develop
PEXA, an agent comprising three specialized sub-
agents: (1) Planner: Decomposes the original prob-
lem into a set of self-contained, simpler questions

Our contributions include:
• We reformulate the text-to-SQL task within
the context of software testing and introduce
parallelism to achieve better Pareto optimality
between the latency and performance;
• We develop an agent, PEXA, to operationalize
our proposed formulation and validate it by
achieving the state-of-the-art1 on the complex
Spider 2.0 benchmark.

Related Work
Here, we provide a brief overview of related work,
with additional details in Appendix A.
Text-to-SQL
Spider 1.0 (Yu et al., 2018) and
BIRD (Li et al., 2023) serve as foundational
datasets for text-to-SQL, whereas Spider 2.0 (Lei
et al., 2025) is a recent, more challenging dataset to
better evaluate methods on real-world cases. While
initial works focused on fine-tuning (Scholak et al.,
2021; Li et al., 2024b), advances in LLMs intro-
duced better prompting-based methods (Pourreza
and Rafiei, 2023). Recent frameworks also explore
agents (Xie et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a) and
inference-time scaling (Lee et al., 2025; Deng et al.,
2025) to tackle complex text-to-SQL. Similarly, we
focus on building an agent but use test cases as a
way to interact with databases.
Latency-Performance Trade-off
Prior work has
explored simple task decomposition (Zhou et al.,
2023b; Khot et al., 2023) and sequential reason-
ing (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023a; Zhou
et al., 2023a) to improve model performance. How-
ever, they require sequential execution and can in-
crease latency. Task decomposition is also lim-
ited to explore only sub-tasks within the original
query, whereas our test cases explore a wider sur-
face of the database robustly and provide the final
SQL generation with extensive grounded context.
Inference-time scaling (Wang et al., 2023b; Light-
man et al., 2024) and breadth-search (Saha et al.,
2024; Lu et al., 2025) enable multi-path search, but
provide limited control over directions and thus
are not efficient. Our parallel exploration offers
simple single-step parallel execution and a better
guided multi-path search, providing an efficient,
low-latency setting without degrading final SQL
generation quality.
Software Testing
Robust systems are built not
by solving the full complexity of a program at once,
but by ensuring that its behavior satisfies a broad
suite of targeted tests (Reid, 2005; Pressman, 2005).
The philosophy to “cover” specific functional re-
quirements lies at the core of modern testing and
test-driven development practices (Fowler, 2002;
Beck, 2003).
3
Approach
3.1
A Software Testing Perspective
Inspired by software testing, we formulate text-to-
SQL as a test coverage problem: creating a set of
simpler, self-contained unit test cases that collec-
tively “cover” the semantics of the user query and
validate against the database. Different from query
decomposition (Deng et al., 2025, inter alia) where
semantics present in sub-queries always reside in
the original query, our testing paradigm covers a
larger semantic surface via tests that extend beyond
the original query to derive and explore additional
information present in the database. We encode
this philosophy in PEXA as described in Figure 1.
3.1.1
Sub-Agents
Planner
The Planner implements the Test Plan-
ning and Modularization principle in software test-
ing (Parnas, 1972), determining the different se-
mantic requirements of the user query and sur-
rounding it with a suite of simpler verifiable (unit)
test cases. In our framework, we define a test case
as a self-contained SQL query that validates seman-
tics present in or related to the user query – such
as a particular filter, join, aggregation, or existence
check – and provides independent and diverse ev-
idence toward reconstructing the full SQL for the
user query.
In addition, the Planner serves as the central con-
trol module, orchestrating the interaction between
the Test Case Generator and the SQL Proposer.
Such interactions are performed through test cases
and their execution results. The Planner determines
when to continue exploratory test-case generation,
and when sufficient evidence has been accumulated
to invoke the Proposer for final SQL synthesis. It
also performs a final verification step, assessing the

Test Case Generator
The Test Case Generator
sub-agent corresponds to the Test Execution phase
in software testing (Ammann and Offutt, 2008),
where individual test cases are instantiated and run
to gather empirical evidence. The Test Case Gener-
ator translates each Planner-issued NL test case into
an executable SQL query. Given the potentially
large and heterogeneous database, we follow Re-
FoRCE (Deng et al., 2025) to perform lightweight
LLM-based schema linking and database compres-
sion, identifying the relevant tables/columns re-
quired for the main user query with a focus on
recall. Conditioned on this pruned schema context,
the sub-agent then synthesizes a precise SQL for
each test case. Importantly, we link the sub-agent
with the SQL Executor tool to build a feedback
mechanism, verifying that the generated SQL exe-
cutes successfully and entails the NL test case.
SQL Proposer
The SQL Proposer sub-agent
aligns with the Test Integration stage in software
testing (Ammann and Offutt, 2008), where the re-
sults of multiple unit test cases are consolidated to
derive the system’s overall intended behavior. In
our framework, given the executed test cases and
the original user query, the SQL Proposer synthe-
sizes the final long-form SQL by combining the
partial semantic signals surfaced through the test-
case results. To maintain a focused and efficient
context, the Proposer is intentionally not supplied
with full database metadata and instead relies solely
on the distilled evidence provided by the test cases.
The module is further equipped with the same SQL
Executor and a Semantic Verifier to ensure both
valid execution and semantic fidelity before return-
ing the final SQL.
3.1.2
Tools
SQL Executor
The SQL Executor tool uses a
SQL execution engine to execute the query on the
database. Based on the execution, it provides three
kinds of feedback: (1) Compilation Error, if there is
a syntax issue, (2) NULL Error, if the SQL executes
but produces zero results, and (3) Success, if the
SQL executes with non-zero results, along with the
truncated executed results.
Semantic Verifier
This tool utilizes an LLM to
ensure alignment between the NL instruction and
generated SQL. To do this, the proposed SQL is
first back-translated into natural language, and then
compared to the original user query to identify any
semantic disparities. If a huge disparity is found,
the tool returns a semantic error.
3.2
Parallel Exploration
Another major advantage of adopting a software
testing perspective is that test cases are inherently
parallelizable. We exploit such parallel exploration
in PEXA to boost performance and latency in three
different ways, as described below.
3


Diverse Test Case Planning
Our Planner pre-
pares the user query with a suite of independent,
self-contained test cases, running the entire plan-
ning phase in a single forward pass. This parallel
testing plan not only lowers planning overhead but
also yields a more diverse set of semantic test cases,
improving downstream coverage.
Parallel Test Case Execution
Since the test
cases are designed to not interact with each other,
Test Case Generator can run all of them in parallel.
This parallel execution increases semantic breadth
without scaling end-to-end latency, analogous to
running a fully parallel test suite rather than a se-
quential battery of checks.
Single-step Multi-path Search
For each test
case being generated, we prompt PEXA to pro-
duce multiple candidate SQL queries with diverse
reasoning strategies in one LLM generation call,
enabling a structured multi-path search without se-
quential calls. This single-step branching expands
the search frontier early, allowing rapid pruning
of weak hypotheses and more efficient exploration
compared to sequential multi-solution exploration
(Yao et al., 2023a). This parallelization strategy
bounds the time complexity to the slowest explored
path, rather than the sum of all paths in an iterative
framework.

Experiments and Results
Dataset
We evaluate on the complex text-to-SQL
Spider 2.0 benchmark, specifically on the Snow
and Lite* versions. Spider 2.0-Snow comprises
547 examples that span 150+ databases, with an av-
erage of 800 columns per database in the Snowflake
dialect. Spider 2.0-Lite* is a Lite version of the
dataset, excluding the examples from BigQuery.2

to consider Execution Accuracy (EX) and EX@4

latency measurement, we report average wall time

Component Ablation
We ablate various compo-
nents used by our framework in Table 2 (more de-
tails about model setup explained in Appendix C.4).
Parallelization components are the most significant
ones towards performance, while the semantic ver-
ifier and proposer also contribute to performance
to some extent. This analysis also demonstrates
how the parallelization branching factor can be con-
trolled for faster inference and lower model costs
while incurring merely 2-3% performance drop.
Studying LLM Synergies
The components used
by our agent can utilize different LLMs, enabling
ablations of different LLMs and their synergies
when used together. In Table 3, we study such ef-
fects with four LLMs.5 With our agent setup, we
found that GPT-o3 and GPT-5 perform the best,
while Claude models are slightly underperforming.
Component-wise ablations with Claude Sonnet-4
over GPT-o3 baseline revealed that Claude per-
forms well on planning, while being poor at long-
context/horizon reasoning for SQL generation. The
ability to combine different models allows a fine-
grained control for our agent to achieve a better
balance between performance and latency.

Error Analysis
We analyzed a sample of failure
cases by comparing generated queries against gold
reference SQL queries shown in Figure 2. The
breakdown reveals that semantic misinterpretations
and flaws in initial planning/approaches are the
dominant error sources, rather than simple syntac-
tic mistakes. These high-level reasoning failures
represent the primary bottleneck and suggest that
future iterations should prioritize improved ques-
tion comprehension and improve search in plans.
5
Conclusion and Future Work
In this work, we present PEXA, a text-to-SQL
agent composed of a Planner, Test Case Gener-
ator, and SQL Proposer sub-agents.
By utiliz-
ing parallelized exploration, PEXA efficiently tra-
verses the search space even under strict latency
constraints. Empirically, we demonstrate that our
approach achieved state-of-the-art results on Spi-
der 2.0 while maintaining wall-time comparable
to existing baselines. Future works can explore
adapting our parallelized agentic architecture for
wider benchmarking on other Text-to-SQL datasets,
as well as broader software engineering and code
generation tasks.

Limitations
Our baselines represent the state-of-the-art as of
November 2025. While newer approaches may
have emerged since, our baseline analysis is con-
strained as these methods are not open, prevent-
ing fair benchmarking. Apart, we do not conduct
any post-training while developing our framework.
While post-training can improve the agentic capa-
bilities of the base LLM, we believe it can hamper
the robustness. Future works can explore better
post-training with PEXA.
Ethical Considerations
Our framework utilizes state-of-the-art LLMs like
GPT-o3 off-the-shelf, and we do not filter/check for
bias mitigation while using these LLMs. For prac-
tical utility, it is advised to consider separate bias
mitigation strategies. Also, since our framework is
agentic in nature, it generates many LLM calls for
the various agentic actions. Thus, running PEXA
can be computationally expensive and should be
considered accordingly. We also acknowledge the
utilization of LLMs/AI for paper writing and cod-
ing.

A
Additional Related Work
We provide a broader related work and the relative
position of our work here.
Datasets for Text-to-SQL
One of the promi-
nent datasets utilized for Text-to-SQL is Spider
1.0 (Yu et al., 2018). Subsequent works also cre-
ated various variants like Spider-Realistic (Deng
et al., 2021), Spider-DK (Gan et al., 2021), and
Spider-SS (Gan et al., 2022). To make the datasets
more realistic and domain-specific, various new
datasets like BIRD (Li et al., 2023), BookSQL (Ku-
mar et al., 2024), and MultiSQL (Li et al., 2024a).
Some works have also focused on specific domains
with datasets like MIMICSQL (Wang et al., 2020b),
BioMedSQL (Koretsky et al., 2025), and LogicCat
(Liu et al., 2025). To combine various challenges
and create a complex industry-scale dataset, Spi-
der 2.0(Lei et al., 2025) was proposed, and we
evaluate our framework on this dataset in our work.
Automating
Text-to-SQL
Pre-LLM
works
(Wang et al., 2020a; Lin et al., 2020; Yin et al.,
2020; Arcadinho et al., 2022) majorly relied on
fine-tuning pre-trained language models on a set
of training data. The advent of LLMs introduced
basic constraint-decoding and prompting methods
(Scholak et al., 2021; Trummer, 2022; Liu et al.,
2023).
Some works focused on improving
in-context examples (Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023;
Nan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a), utilizing
retrieval-augmented generation (Guo et al., 2023;
Talaei et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024), and inference-
time scaling (Lee et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025;
Pourreza et al., 2025). With more compute, some
works also show the effectiveness of fine-tuning
small and large LLMs for text-to-SQL (Pourreza
and Rafiei, 2024; Thorpe et al., 2024; He et al.,
2025; Yao et al., 2025). Recent works have also
proposed the use of multi-agent frameworks (Xie
et al., 2024; Cen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024b,
2025a) to tackle complex SQL queries. Utilization
of semantic verifiers Sawhney et al. (2025) have
also been explored lately. In our work, we work
on similar directions by proposing a simple
multi-agent framework PEXA for the Spider 2.0
benchmark.
Analogy to Software Testing
Software testing
provides the conceptual backbone for the formu-
lation of our agentic framework PEXA. Classical
works formalize software-testing as specification,
coverage, and evidence aggregation rather than
exhaustive verification, and emphasize designing
suites of targeted tests to characterize system be-
havior (Reid, 2005; Pressman, 2005). Subsequent
works have unified these ideas into rigorous cover-
age criteria, automated test execution, and oracle-
based evaluation for determining correctness from
multiple test outcomes (Ammann and Offutt, 2008).
Our work also draws inspiration from the concept
of executable specifications, central to test-driven
development and agile engineering (Beck, 2003).
Structural and data-flow testing works also show
how carefully chosen, small test units provide max-
imal information about program semantics (Rapps
and Weyuker, 1985). Overall, we root our concep-
tual design choices deeply in software testing.
Parallelization in LLMs
Decomposition in plan-
ning (Zhou et al., 2023b; Khot et al., 2023; Wang
et al., 2023a) improves model performance; how-
ever, the co-dependent plans demand sequential
execution and can increase the latency. Newer ap-
proaches (Saha et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025) have
explored parallel execution-based planning, how-
ever only in limited settings like evaluation and
constrained generation where subtasks are more
explicit. Other works (Parekh et al., 2025c; Pan
et al., 2025) explore dynamic planning of model
reasoning methods to improve search. Sequential
reasoning (Wei et al., 2022) and various multi-
path breadth search approaches (Yao et al., 2023a;
Besta et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023a) iteratively
explore each node, which increases latency. On
the other side, inference-time scaling approaches
(Wang et al., 2023b; Lightman et al., 2024) that
utilize temperature for multi-path search offer little
control over the diversity in approaches, rendering
them inefficient. In our work, we propose paral-
lel exploration, which offers the benefits of simple
single-step parallel executable decomposition and
a better guided multi-path search in an efficient,
low-latency setting.

In Table 14, we demonstrate an end-to-end case

explore one datapoint. Overall, the trajectory has

Directions for Future Work
In our work, we provide a strong proof-of-concept
for parallelized exploration to improve the Pareto
optimality of performance-latency in text-to-SQL
on Spider 2.0. As part of future work, it would
be imperative to provide the generalizability of
this paradigm across other text-to-SQL datasets
like SPIDER (Yu et al., 2018) and BIRD (Li et al.,
2023). To this end, exploring post-training of indi-
vidual components of our agentic workflow would
be required. Synthetic data generation methods
(Duan et al., 2025; Parekh et al., 2025a) should also
be explored to this end to support this post-training.
At a broader scale, works can also explore utiliz-
ing this framework for broader set of tasks in code
generation, tool-calling, and beyond (Wang et al.,
2025b; Barres et al., 2025; Parekh et al., 2024).

Abstract: LLM-based agents for text-to-SQL often strug- gle with a latency-performance trade-off, where performance improvements come at the cost of latency or vice versa. We cast text-to-SQL generation as a problem of passing software test coverage. Similar to its counterpart in soft- ware engineering, the original query is prepared with a suite of test cases with simpler, atomic SQL queries that are executed in parallel and together ensure semantic coverage of the origi- nal query. After iterating on test case coverage, the final SQL is generated only when enough information is gathered, using the explored test case SQL queries to ground the final generation. We validated our framework on a state-of-the- art benchmark for text-to-SQL, Spider 2.0 (Lei et al., 2025), achieving a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 70.2%. 1
